title: Big to Small Converter
context: Grade 5, the pages on changing a bigger unit of time into a smaller one. An adult sees a multiplication with a sum after it. What the pages are doing is making every conversion a matter of how many of the smaller unit fit into one of the bigger, where the number is 24 or 60 and never 10, and the leftover part is simply added on.

writeup.why: Change days into hours, hours into minutes and minutes into seconds by multiplying by 24 or 60 and adding the leftover part, and change a fraction of an hour into minutes.
writeup.look: A unit ladder of four rungs with deep blue bars on it, a Break down button, a tray for the leftover part and, on the last phase, a bar of one hour cut into sixty cells.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Big to Small Converter' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of bars broken down. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The unit ladder of four rungs, days, hours, minutes and seconds, stands down the left of the area at x 90 from y 230 to y 690, each rung 115 tall, with the unit fact beside each step in violet, labelled Regroup. The bars the question gives are deep blue, labelled Given, on the rung they use, one for each whole unit, with the leftover smaller part waiting in a small tray at x 520, y 240. The Break down button stands at x 900, y 230, and each press splits every bar of the bigger unit into that many bars of the next rung down, which slide across the working area in rows of the same length. The multiplication is written in ink under the rows along y 620 as the bars are made. The leftover tray is dragged in among the new bars, amber while it is being added, and the total is read in green, labelled Answer, at x 520, y 680 with its unit. On the fourth phase the bar of one hour, 720 wide, lies along y 300 cut into sixty minute cells, and the cells of the fraction the child shades are amber while they are counted. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a delete key, and keys for days, h, min and s. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the nine tools of this chapter share them. What the question gives, as a clock time, a length of time, a start date or a number of days, is deep blue, labelled Given or Start. What the working reaches, as an end time, a length of time, a converted time or a date, is green, labelled Answer, End or How long. The thin second hand and the seconds it counts are vermilion, labelled Second hand. One jump along a time line, and one regrouped unit carried or borrowed, are violet, labelled Jump, Carry or Regroup. On a day bar the half from noon until just before midnight is rose, labelled p.m., and the half from midnight until just before noon stays warm white inside its outline, labelled a.m. The hand, digit, column, jump or date being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open, labelled Place holder, and for nothing else. The hour hand and the minute hand, dials, tick marks, time lines, arrows, operation signs and step labels are near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength. Chrome never borrows one of the content colours, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The last length of time stays on the ladder with its bars broken down, the leftover part dropped in and the total beside it in green.

phases.win: the hour bars are counted and the total turns green, with its unit
phases.does: presses Break down to split each day bar into twenty-four hour bars, then drops the leftover hours in and adds
phases.goal: 1 day is 24 h, so multiply the days by 24 and add the leftover hours
phases.says: How many hours in one day? Break down every day bar.
phases.check: Away from the screen: how many hours are there in two days, and which unit fact do you say first?
phases.feels: each bar breaking into a row of shorter bars and the row counting up
phases.hands: Cut a paper strip for one day and a shorter strip for one hour. Fold the day strip until it holds as many hour strips as a day has, count them, then lay the leftover hour strips beside them.
phases.tries: First rung: break one day into hours and count them. Second rung: break two days and add a few leftover hours. Third rung: the same task with three days and a few hours, before the question's own length returns.

writeup.delight: On the first phase, as the Break down button is pressed, each day bar splits into hour bars that slide apart and settle into rows of the same length, and the total counts up in green as the last bar lands.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet broken down. On the first phase the ladder holds a length in days and hours as deep blue bars, with the Break down button beside it and the leftover hours waiting in a small tray. On the second the ladder holds a length in hours and minutes, and on the third a length in minutes and seconds. On the fourth a bar of one hour lies whole above the ladder beside a mixed number of hours in deep blue. One thing moves, once: the Break down button or the bar of one hour gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.
writeup.freePlay: Any length of time set on the ladder and broken down to any smaller rung, and any fraction of an hour shaded. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on days into hours, hours into minutes, minutes into seconds and a part of an hour.
voiceLines: A bar of time on a ladder, ready to break down.
How many hours in one day? Break down every day bar.
Sixty minutes to an hour. Break down each bar, then drop in the minutes left over.
Sixty seconds to a minute. Do you need the minutes first?
Shade the part of the hour. How many minute cells is that?
A new length of time. Break it down the same way.
Free play. Set any length of time and break it down.
Count the new bars again. Did any bar stay unbroken?
You broke bigger units into smaller ones and added the leftover part.

observations.why: 1 day is 24 h, and the same number fits into every day.
observations.soWhat: multiply the days by 24, then add the leftover hours.
observations.observe: Every day bar broke into the same number of hour bars.

observations.why: the leftover part is already in minutes, so it needs no breaking down.
observations.soWhat: multiply only the whole hours by 60, then add the leftover minutes.
observations.observe: The leftover minutes dropped in beside the new minute bars and were counted once.

observations.why: 1 h is 60 min and 1 min is 60 s, and the ladder has a rung for each unit.
observations.soWhat: change one step at a time, and the answer is a bigger number than the one given.
observations.observe: A length in hours turned into minutes before it turned into seconds.

observations.why: a fraction of an hour is that fraction of 60 min.
observations.soWhat: the whole hours give their minutes, the shaded part gives the rest, and the two are added.
observations.observe: The shaded cells of the hour bar were counted as minutes and joined the minutes of the whole hours.

serves.exercise: converting four lengths of time in days and hours into hours
converting four lengths of time in hours and minutes into minutes

finding in seconds the time a show gives to advertisements

source_tool.description: A unit ladder of four rungs, days, hours, minutes and seconds, stands down the left of the working area, with the unit fact beside each step in violet, labelled Regroup: 1 day is 24 h, 1 h is 60 min and 1 min is 60 s. The length of time the question gives is set in deep blue bars, labelled Given, on the rung it uses, one bar for each whole unit, with the leftover smaller part waiting in a small tray beside them. A Break down button splits every bar of the bigger unit into that many bars of the next rung down, and the multiplication is written under the ladder as it happens. The leftover part is then dropped in among the new bars and the two are added. The total is read in green, labelled Answer, with its unit. On the last phase a bar of one hour is cut into sixty minute cells, a fraction of the hour is shaded, and its cells are counted as minutes. The running count at the top left of the canvas counts the bars broken down.
source_tool.art_direction: Long bars snapped into short blocks / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: round clock faces with twelve numbers and sixty small marks, a day bar from midnight to midnight, a time line with jumps, columns of hours, minutes and seconds, and month calendars with seven columns.

Every clock time is written in one notation: 4:15 p.m. for a 12-hour time, with a colon and a.m. or p.m., and 1615 hours for a 24-hour time, four digits and the word hours, never a colon and never a dot. Noon is written 12 noon and midnight 12 midnight. A length of time is written 2 h 15 min, 3 days 5 h and 40 s, or in words, and never as a clock time.

Every hour hand sits at its true angle: it moves on from each number as the minutes pass, so at a quarter past it has gone a quarter of the way to the next number. The minute hand is long, the hour hand short and thick, and the second hand thin, longer than both and vermilion. Label lines stay outside the dial.
A time line that passes 12 midnight shows midnight as its own mark and says the next day after it. A count of days always says whether both the first and the last day are counted.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: hands turning, a jump along a time line, a carried unit moving to the next column, or dates being counted on a calendar.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a hand, a digit, a jump or a date the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a time plays in a piece of working: what the question gives, a clock time, a length of time, a start date or a number of days, is deep blue, and what the working reaches, an end time, a length of time, a converted time or a date, is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The thin second hand and the seconds it counts are vermilion. One jump along a time line, and one regrouped unit carried or borrowed, is violet. The half of the day from noon until just before midnight is rose on a day bar, and the half from midnight until just before noon stays warm white inside its outline. The hand, digit, column, jump or date being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open at the front of a 24-hour time. The hour hand and the minute hand are near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Second hand, Jump, Carry, a.m., p.m., Noon and Midnight, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Count the new bars again. Did any bar stay unbroken?
voice.onNext: A new length of time. Break it down the same way.
voice.opening: A bar of time on a ladder, ready to break down.
voice.onFinish: You broke bigger units into smaller ones and added the leftover part.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Set any length of time and break it down.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has counted the minutes in a few hours on a clock face, and has said how many of the smaller unit make one of the bigger. The tool is what breaks each bar into the smaller unit and adds the leftover part, which a printed multiplication cannot show.

answer_key.rule: To change a bigger unit into a smaller one, multiply. 1 day is 24 h, 1 h is 60 min and 1 min is 60 s. Multiply the whole bigger units by 24 or by 60, then add the leftover smaller part. A length of time in hours, minutes and seconds is changed one step at a time, from hours to minutes and then to seconds. A fraction of an hour is that fraction of 60 min. The answer is a bigger number than the one given, because more of the smaller unit are needed.
answer_key.wrong: The stage keeps the child's working. A bar of the bigger unit left unbroken stays, lit amber, beside the bars of the smaller unit the child has made from the others. A leftover part left out of the total shows its tray still full, lit amber. A fraction of an hour cut into the wrong number of parts stays, and the sixty cells of the hour are lit amber beside it. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: 1 day is 24 h, so multiply the days by 24.
items.question: How many hours are there in 9 days 5 h?
items.checkpoint: To change days into hours, multiply the days by 24, then add the leftover hours.
items.misconception: Adding 24 to the number of days instead of multiplying by 24, which gives far too few hours.

steps: 1 h is 60 min, so multiply the hours by 60.
items.question: How many minutes are there in 5 h 50 min?
items.checkpoint: To change hours into minutes, multiply the hours by 60, then add the leftover minutes.
items.misconception: Leaving out the leftover minutes, and giving only the minutes that the whole hours make.

steps: 1 min is 60 s, so multiply the minutes by 60.
items.question: How many seconds are there in 26 min 15 s?
items.checkpoint: To change minutes into seconds, multiply the minutes by 60, then add the leftover seconds.
items.misconception: Multiplying the leftover seconds by 60 as well, so they are counted many times over.

steps: A fraction of an hour is that fraction of 60 min.
3/4 of 60 is 45, so 3/4 h is 45 min.
items.question: How many minutes are there in 3 3/4 h?
items.checkpoint: A fraction of an hour is that fraction of 60 min, and a bigger unit is changed into a smaller one by multiplying.
items.misconception: Putting the two numbers of the fraction side by side and taking 3/4 h for 34 min, instead of taking 3/4 of 60.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: How many hours are there in 2 days 6 h?
How many minutes are there in 4 h 10 min?
How many seconds are there in 6 min?
How many hours are there in 12 days 20 h?
How many minutes are there in 6 h 45 min?
How many seconds are there in 1 h 5 min? Change the hours to minutes first.
items.final_answer: 3900 s, because 1 h 5 min is 65 min and 65 x 60 = 3900

items.question: Which is longer, 2 3/4 h or 150 min?
items.final_answer: 2 3/4 h, because 2 3/4 h is 165 min, and that is more than 150 min

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

teaching_notes: Say the unit fact aloud before every conversion: 1 day is 24 h, 1 h is 60 min, 1 min is 60 s. Multiply the whole bigger units, then add the leftover smaller part, and say both steps. The answer is a bigger number than the one given, so ask the child to check that it is. A length in hours, minutes and seconds is changed one step at a time. A fraction of an hour is that fraction of 60 min, as the fractions chapter taught. Keep 1 day as 24 h.
